question.text: A wire carrying current I has the shape as shown in adjoining figure. Linear parts of the wire are very long and parallel to $\mathrm{X}$ -axis while semicircular portion of radius $\mathrm{R}$ is lying in Y-Z plane. Magnetic field at point $\mathrm{O}$ is:

question.text:
A long straight wire along the $Z$ -axis carries a current I in the negative $Z$ -direction. The

magnetic vector field $\vec{B}$ at a point having coordinates $(x, y)$ in the $Z=0$ plane is

solution.text:
The wire carries a current $I$ in the negative $z$ -direction. We have to consider the magnetic vector field $\vec{B}$ at $(x, y)$ in the $z=0$ plane.
Magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to $O P$ $\therefore \vec{B}=B \sin \theta \hat{i}-B \cos \theta \hat{j}$ $$ \begin{array}{l} \sin \theta=\frac{y}{r}, \cos \theta=\frac{x}{r} B=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi r} \\ \therefore \quad \vec{B}=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi r^{2}}(y \hat{i}-x \hat{j}) \end{array} $$ or $\quad \vec{B}=\frac{\mu_{0} I(y \hat{i}-x \hat{j})}{2 \pi\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)}$

question.text: The straight wire $A B$ carries a current $I$. The ends of the wire subtend angles $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ at the point $P$ as shown in figure. The magnetic field at the point $P$ is

solution.text: The magnetic field at a point $P$ due to a current carrying straight wire, such that the ends of the wires, makes angle $\alpha$ and $\beta$ (see figure) is given by $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi d}(\sin \alpha-\sin \beta)$ where, $d$ is the distance between the point $P$ and wire. In the given problem, $\alpha=\theta_1$ and $\beta=\theta_2$ $\therefore \quad B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi d}\left(\sin \theta_1-\sin \theta_2\right)$

question.text: A long straight wire of radius a carries a steady current 1 . The current is uniformly distributed across its cross section. The ratio of the magnetic field at $\frac{\mathrm{a}}{2}$ and 2a from axis of the wire is:

solution.text:
Magnetic field due to straight wire,
$B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}$
Magnetic field at $\frac{a}{2}$ is,
$\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{a} / 2}=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi(\mathrm{a} / 2)}$
$\therefore \frac{\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{a} / 2}}{\mathrm{~B}_{2 \mathrm{a}}}=\frac{1}{1}=1: 1$

question.text: A solenoid of 1200 turns is wound uniformly in a single layer on a glass tube $2 \mathrm{~m}$ long and $0.2 \mathrm{~m}$ in diameter. The magnetic intensity at the center of the solenoid when a current of 2 A flows through it is:

solution.text:
Given that number of turns, $n=1200$
Current, $\mathrm{I}=2 \mathrm{~A}$
Magnetic field at centre inside the solenoid is given by,
$\mathrm{B}=\mu_0 \mathrm{nI}$
So magnetic intensity at centre of the solenoid,
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{H}=\frac{\mathrm{B}}{\mu_0}=\mathrm{nI}=\left(\frac{1200}{2}\right)(2) \quad\left(\because \mathrm{B}=\mu_0 \mathrm{H}\right) \\
& \mathrm{H}=1.2 \times 10^3 \mathrm{Am}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$

question.text: A solenoid is $2 \mathrm{~m}$ long and $3 \mathrm{~cm}$ in diameter. It has 5 layers of winding of 1000 turns each and carries a current of $5 \mathrm{~A}$. What is the magnetic field at its centre ? Use the standard value of $\mu_{0}$.

solution.text:
Length of solenoid, $l=2 \mathrm{~m}$

Total number of turns, $\mathrm{N}=5 \times 1000=5000$

Number of turns per unit length,

$\mathrm{n}=\frac{\mathrm{N}}{l}=\frac{5000}{2}=2500 \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$

Current, I = 5A

Now, B $=\mu_{0} \mathrm{nI}=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2500 \times 5 \mathrm{~T}$

$=1.57 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~T}$

question.text: Two parallel conductors carry current in opposite directions as shown in figure. One conductor carries a current of $10.0 \mathrm{~A}$. Point $\mathrm{C}$ is a distance $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}$ to the right of the $10.0 \mathrm{~A}$ current. If $\mathrm{d}=18 \mathrm{~cm}$ and I is adjusted so that the magnetic field at $\mathrm{Cis}$ zero, the value of the current $I$ is

solution.text:
The magnetic field at $\mathrm{C}$ due to first conductor

is $\mathrm{B}_{1}=\frac{\mu_{0}}{2 \pi} \frac{\mathrm{I}}{3 \mathrm{~d} / 2}$ (since, point $\mathrm{C}$ is separated

by $\mathrm{d}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}=\frac{3 \mathrm{~d}}{2}$ from 1 st conductor). The direction of field is perpendicular to the plane of paper and directed outwards. The magnetic field at $\mathrm{C}$ due to second conductor is $\mathrm{B}_{2}=\frac{\mu_{0}}{2 \pi} \frac{10}{\mathrm{~d} / 2}$ (since, point $\mathrm{C}$

is separated by $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}$ from 2 nd conductor) The direction of field is perpendicular to the plane of paper and directed inwards. Since, direction of $\mathrm{B}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{B}_{2}$ at point $\mathrm{C}$ is in opposite direction and the magnetic field at C is zero, therefore,

$$

\begin{array}{c}

\mathrm{B}_{1}=\mathrm{B}_{2} \\

\frac{\mu_{0}}{2 \pi} \frac{\mathrm{I}}{3 \mathrm{~d} / 2}=\frac{\mu_{0}}{2 \pi} \frac{10}{\mathrm{~d} / 2}

\end{array}

$$

On solving $\mathrm{I}=30.0 \mathrm{~A}$

question.text: A horizontal overhead powerline is at height of $4 \mathrm{~m}$ from the ground and carries a current of $100 \mathrm{~A}$ from east to west. The magnetic field directly below it on the ground is $\left(\mu_{0}=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{Tm} \mathrm{A}^{-1}\right)$

solution.text:
The magnetic field is $\mathrm{B}=\frac{\mu_{0}}{4 \pi} \frac{2 \mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{r}}=10^{-7} \times \frac{2 \times 100}{4}=5 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~T}$
According to right hand palm rule, the magnetic field is directed towards south.

question.text: A charge particle is moving in a uniform magnetic field $(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}) \mathrm{T}$. If it has an acceleration of $(\alpha \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^2$, then the value of $\alpha$ will be :

solution.text:
Given that uniform magnetic field, $\vec{B}=(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}) T$
Acceleration $\vec{a}=(\alpha \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ We know that
$F=q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) \Rightarrow m \vec{a}=q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$
Here, $\vec{a} \perp \vec{B}$, so, $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{B}=0$
$(\alpha \hat{i}-4 \hat{j})(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j})=0 \Rightarrow 2 \alpha-12=0 \Rightarrow \alpha=6$

question.text: Two particles $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ having equal charges, after being accelerated through the same potential difference, enter a region of uniform magnetic field and describe circular paths of radii $\mathrm{R}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{R}_{2}$, respectively. The ratio of masses of $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ is

solution.text:
When a charge particle is allowed to move in a uniform magnetic field, then it describes spiral or circular path

$$

\begin{array}{l}

\text { Centripetal force, } \frac{\mathrm{mv}^{2}}{\mathrm{R}}=\mathrm{qvB} \quad \therefore \\

\mathrm{v}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{qB}}{\mathrm{m}} \mathrm{R}\right) \\

\text { Hence, } \sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{q} \mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{m}}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{qB}}{\mathrm{m}}\right) \mathrm{R}\left[\because \mathrm{V}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{qV}}{\mathrm{m}}}\right] \\

\Rightarrow \mathrm{R}=\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{mV}}{\mathrm{q}}\right)^{1 / 2} \times \frac{1}{\mathrm{~B}} \\

\text { or, } \mathrm{m} \propto \mathrm{R}^{2}

\end{array}

$$

$[\because \mathrm{V}, \mathrm{q}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ are constant $]$

$$

\text { or, } \frac{\mathrm{m}_{1}}{\mathrm{~m}_{2}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}_{1}}{\mathrm{R}_{2}}\right)^{2}

$$

question.text: A charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field and losses $4 \%$ of its kinetic energy. The radius of curvature of its path changes by

solution.text:
As we know $\mathrm{F}=\mathrm{qvB}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}^{2}}{\mathrm{r}}$

$\therefore \mathrm{r}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}}{\mathrm{Bq}}$

And $\mathrm{KE}=\mathrm{k}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^{2}$

$\therefore \mathrm{mv}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~km}}$

$\therefore \mathrm{r}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}}{\mathrm{qB}}=\frac{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~km}}}{\mathrm{qB}}$

$\Rightarrow r \propto \sqrt{k}$ or $r=c^{1 / 2}(c$ is a constant $)$ $\frac{\mathrm{dr}}{\mathrm{dr}}=\mathrm{c} \frac{\mathrm{dk}^{1 / 2}}{\mathrm{dr}}$ or $\frac{\mathrm{c} \Delta \mathrm{k}}{\Delta \mathrm{r}}=2 \sqrt{\mathrm{k}}$

$\frac{\Delta r}{r}=\frac{\mathrm{c} \Delta \mathrm{k}}{2 \sqrt{\mathrm{k}} \mathrm{c} \sqrt{\mathrm{k}}}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{k}}{2 \mathrm{k}}$

Therefore percentage changes in radius of path,

$\frac{\Delta r}{r} \times 100=\frac{\Delta k}{2 k} \times 100=2 \%$

question.text: A narrow beam of protons and deuterons, each having the same momentum, enters a region of uniform magnetic field directed perpendicular to their direction of momentum. The ratio of the radii of the circular paths described by them is

solution.text:
Since, the radius of circular path of a charged

particle in magnetic field is $\mathrm{r}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}}{\mathrm{qB}}=\frac{\rho}{\mathrm{qB}}$

Now, the radius of circular path of charged particle of given momentum $\rho$ and magnetic field $\mathrm{B}$ is given by $\mathrm{r} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{q}}$

But charge on both charged particles, protons and deuterons, is same. Therefore,

$$

\frac{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{D}}}=\frac{\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{D}}}{\mathrm{q}_{\rho}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{l}}

$$

question.text: The magnetic moments associated with two closely wound circular coils A and B of radius $r_A=10 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $r_B=20 \mathrm{~cm}$ respectively are equal if: (Where $\mathrm{N}_A, \mathrm{I}_A$ and $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{B}}, \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{B}}$ are number of turn and current of $A$ and $B$ respectively)

solution.text:
The magnetic moment associated with circular coil,
$\begin{aligned}
& M=N I A \\
& M_A=M_B \\
& \therefore N_A I_A A_A=N_B I_B A_B \\
& \therefore N_A I_A \pi(0.1)^2=N_B I_B \pi(0.2)^2\left(\because A=\pi r^2\right) \\
& \therefore N_A I_A=4 N_B I_B
\end{aligned}$

question.text: The magnetic moment of an electron (e) revolving in an orbit around nucleus with an orbital angular momentum is given by:

solution.text:
As $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}=\mathrm{IA}$
$\Rightarrow|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}|=\frac{\mathrm{e}}{\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{v}}} \pi \mathrm{R}^2$ $\left[\because \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{Q}}{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{\mathrm{e}}{\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{V}}}\right]$
$\Rightarrow|\vec{M}|=\frac{1}{2} e v R \Rightarrow|\vec{M}|=\frac{\mathrm{mvR}}{1} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{e}}{2 \mathrm{~m}}$
$\Rightarrow|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}|=\frac{\mathrm{eL}}{2 \mathrm{~m}} \Rightarrow|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}|=-\frac{\mathrm{e} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}}{2 \mathrm{~m}}$
[ $\because$ Here $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}$ will always be opposite]

question.text: The ratio of angular momentum <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi></math> to the atomic dipole moment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> for hydrogen like atoms and ions is

always constant and is equal to twice the ratio of mass to the charge of electron to the principal quantum number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math>
proportional to the principal quantum number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math>

solution.text:
The electron moving with a speed v in the circular Bohr orbit of radius r constitutes a current of magnitude.

i=eT. where T is the orbital period of the electron.

T=2πr/v

i=ev2πr

By definition of atomic dipole moment μi, its magnitude is given by

μi=iA=eV2πr·πr2=evr2

∴ Angular momentum, L=mvr
∴ Lμi=2mvrevr=2me= constant

question.text: Magnetic moment of bar magnet is $\mathrm{M}$. The work done to turn the magnet by $90^{\circ}$ of magnet in direction of magnetic field $\mathrm{B}$ will be
